tasks.short: Check the facts against the offence elements, look up the offence code, consult the duty officer and correct the charge in the record.

steps.what: Officer checks the facts in the report against the elements of the offence
Officer looks up the offence code and article in the printed charge list
Officer consults the duty officer to verify that the proper legal charges have been made
Officer types the corrected charge into the record

tasks.design: The police registration system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) offers a searchable offence code list that shows each offence's legal elements and article, and the officer picks the code instead of typing it. Checking the facts and consulting the duty officer stay with people; no software decides a charge.
tasks.previous_blocker: Offence codes were looked up in printed lists and typed by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Registration systems can hold searchable code lists with elements per offence.
tasks.still_hard: Whether facts meet an offence's elements is legal judgement.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that a fight was self-defence, not assault.

reach.learn: Whether element lists reduce routine questions.

evidence.claim: Registration systems can hold searchable offence code lists with legal elements.
Solely automated decisions with adverse effect on a person need prior human intervention under the police data act.

assumptions: Boundary: from the report to the recorded charge; the prosecutor's decision is outside.
Input contract: offence code list and elements kept by the national police's legal department; fallback is the printed list.

Checking facts and consulting keep their full time. s2 keeps 40 because the code is found by search instead of in the printed list and reading the elements stays; s4 keeps 80 because the code is picked instead of copied by hand.
research_questions: Do charge corrections by the prosecutor fall?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: learning the code search is a one-off; the list is kept by the legal department.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: experienced officers know most codes, so the search saves less look-up time (10.5); high: the list is looked up for most charges (18.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Note facts at the scene, get known details filled in, write the report, check it for missing elements, sign it and file it.

steps.what: Officer notes facts in a notebook during the incident
Officer types person, vehicle and location details into the report today; after the change they fill from the incident registration and ID checks and the officer checks them
Officer records facts in the report narrative that documents the incident
Officer rereads the report to find missing facts
Officer checks the final report before signing: facts, narrative, prefilled details and the prosecution file it goes to
Officer signs the checked report under oath and sends it to the prosecution's file: printed and handed in today, sent from the registration system after the change

tasks.design: The report in the police registration system ({OPS_SYSTEM}) fills person, vehicle and location details from the incident registration and ID checks. Rule-based checks per offence type list facts that are still missing, and the officer checks the final report, signs it under oath and sends it to the prosecution from the system. The narrative stays the officer's own writing: a randomised trial found AI-drafted police reports were not written faster.
tasks.previous_blocker: Known details were retyped and missing facts found only when the prosecutor sent the report back.
tasks.enabler_now: Registration systems hold incident data, and rule-based gap checks run in police tools today.
tasks.still_hard: A report under oath must be the officer's own account.
tasks.human_edge: Writing precisely what happened, in a way that holds up in court.

reach.learn: Whether reports come back less often.

evidence.claim: A randomised trial found AI-drafted police reports were not written faster.
A police tool asks fraud victims for missing facts using argumentation logic, not a language model.
High-risk police data processing needs a DPIA, and data on daily tasks are kept at most five years.

assumptions: Boundary: from scene notes to the filed report; the prosecutor's work is outside.
Input contract: incident data from the control room and the officer's checks; gap rules per offence type kept by the national police's legal department; fallback is typing.

The narrative, scene notes and the final check stay manual and keep their full time. s2 keeps 15 for checking prefilled details and typing those not registered; s4 keeps 50 because missing facts are listed and the officer resolves them; signing and sending keep 25.
Prosecution time is outside the officer's savings.
unknowns: Share of reports sent back today.
research_questions: Do reports sent back for missing facts fall?

already_counted.description: Officer resolves facts flagged as missing.

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: checking prefilled details is kept in s2.

approvals.approved_version: The report exactly as checked by the officer in s5, signed under oath and sent once to the prosecution's file for this case in s6; any change needs a new check and signature.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: incident registrations are often incomplete, so about half of the details are still typed (23.0); high: details fill for most reports (31.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Hear the parties and witnesses, examine the scene, check earlier registrations and weigh the facts against the law.

steps.what: Officer hears accounts from the parties involved and witnesses
Officer examines the scene and the evidence
Officer searches several police systems for earlier registrations on the persons and address
Officer reviews facts of incidents to determine if criminal acts or statute violations were involved

tasks.design: One search on the officer's mobile device queries the police registration systems ({OPS_SYSTEM}) the officer is authorised for, instead of separate searches. Hearing accounts, examining the scene and deciding stay with the officer; no score or prediction is shown.
tasks.previous_blocker: Earlier registrations sat in separate systems with separate searches.
tasks.enabler_now: Police systems can be searched through one query layer within access rights.
tasks.still_hard: Earlier registrations can bias judgement; access must follow the police data act.
tasks.human_edge: Reading a tense situation and the people in it.

reach.learn: Whether one search finds links missed before.

evidence.claim: Police systems can be searched through one query layer within access rights.
Predicting offences solely from profiling is banned under the AI Act; this design shows records only.

assumptions: Boundary: from accounts to the offence decision; arrest is outside.
Input contract: access rights set by the national police's information management; fallback is separate searches.
Hearing, examining and deciding do not change.
research_questions: Does one search change what officers find?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: learning the combined search is a one-off.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: some systems the officer needs are not in the combined search, so separate searches stay (3.0); high: one search covers them (6.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Observe and question people on patrol, check persons and vehicles, request camera footage, get the location filled in and register the observation.

steps.what: Officer observes and questions people to investigate suspicious activities on patrol
Officer checks persons and vehicles on the mobile device
Officer finds cameras near the observation and asks for footage: door to door today; after the change from the camera register, knocking only where no camera is registered
Officer checks the footage request: camera, time window, the reason and the owner it goes to
Officer sends the checked online request to the camera owner
Camera owner looks up and hands over the requested footage
Officer looks up and types the street address of the observation today; after the change the device fills it in and the officer checks it
Officer writes a short registration of the observation: typed today, with pick lists after the change

tasks.design: A register of private cameras that owners have chosen to register shows on the officer's device, and the officer checks an online request and sends it to the owner, so fewer doors need knocking. The device fills in the location of a new registration for the officer to check; the officer writes the short registration with pick lists in about the time it takes today. Observing, questioning and checks stay as they are; device location is used for the registration only, not to track officers.
tasks.previous_blocker: Footage was found door to door and addresses typed in by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Police keep registers of private cameras whose owners agree to be contacted; mobile devices know their location.
tasks.still_hard: Many cameras are not registered; location logs could observe officers.
tasks.human_edge: Sensing that something is not right on a quiet street.

reach.learn: Whether register requests bring footage sooner.

evidence.claim: Police keep registers of private cameras whose owners agree to be contacted.
Location logs that show officers' movements need works council consent.

assumptions: Boundary: from observation to registration; follow-up investigation is outside.
Input contract: camera register kept by the national police with owners' consent; pick lists set by the national police; fallback is door to door and typing.

Observing, questioning, checks, writing the registration (a first record) and checking and sending each request keep their full time. s3 keeps 60 for cameras that are not registered; s4 keeps 10 for checking the location.
Camera owners' time is outside the officer's savings.
unknowns: Share of local cameras that are registered.
research_questions: Does footage arrive faster through register requests?

incremental.description: No ongoing upkeep: checking the filled-in location is kept in s4.
New camera owners register their cameras and keep their contact details current; handing over footage is shown in s6.

approvals.approved_version: The footage request with camera, time window and reason exactly as checked by the officer in s3c, sent once to the registered owner of that camera; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: few owners register their cameras, so most footage is still found door to door (6.7); high: many cameras near observations are registered (10.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The patrol officer keeps every judgement on the street and in the report; lookups, retyping and door-to-door footage requests shrink.
role.ambitious_version: An officer whose reports are complete the first time and who spends the saved time on the street.
